review: Cute little deviation from the franchise's main formula. It's like Pokemon, but you kidnap their children instead.

[h1]A distinct take on the Monster Hunter series with a refined “rock, paper, and scissors” mechanic at its core[/h1]

Monster Hunter Stories 2 (MHS2)… another Monster Hunter game on Steam? Don’t mind if I do! I always had a soft spot for turn-based RPGs, which makes MHS2 definitely right up my alley. Capcom took a different approach to the series and made a story-driven Monster Hunter entry with anime-esque visuals. In addition to that, I’m amazed at how they turned the humble “rock, paper, and scissors'' into an interesting combat mechanic. While some parts of it could’ve been better, I thoroughly enjoyed MHS2!

[h2][b]Now, about the game[/b][/h2]
[b] In a nutshell, the reasons I’m particularly fond of Monster Hunter Stories 2 were that: [/b]
[list]
    [*] It’s Monster Hunter, but emphasized the narrative aspect of the game
    [*] Completely different art direction compared with other Monster Hunter entries
    [*] Dynamic turn-based combat with many elements to consider
    [*] Min-maxing options for “monsties” were simple and amusing at the same time  – Yes, they call them monsties instead of monsters
    [*] Co-op quests were very helpful in completing the monsterpedia
[/list]
[h3]The light that changes everything[/h3]
The story begins with what was supposed to be a time for festivities turning grim as an eerie pillar of light bursts out of the ground, causing the guardian of Hakolo island to run amok and disappear, leaving but an egg that could very well be key to our salvation… or destruction. Journey through the beautiful world of Monster Hunter not as a hunter, but as a tamer tasked with unraveling the mystery surrounding the egg, while trying to make sense of what is the meaning behind the eerie pillars of light scattered throughout the continent. 

Unlike the other entries, MHS2's main selling point is that it focuses on the narrative aspect, so storytelling is a lot more enjoyable. Granted, the story caters to a younger audience, but it’s still enjoyable overall. There are two things I don’t particularly like about the story, the first one would be, everytime a new character is introduced, they seem to know and praise the main character’s late grandfather a lot; they just can’t stop mentioning how great he was. The second one is the fact that one of the antagonists was badly written, and by that, I mean horrible. One of them shows up at one point of the story and is never mentioned again until he decides to make a grand reappearance on the final chapter; by that time, I already forgot that he even existed.

MHS2 has a distinct visual style that makes it stand out from the rest of the entries. Capcom’s decision to use cel-shaded visuals was right on the money and it works exceptionally well for this particular kind of RPG. The overworld was lush and a wonder to explore. In fact, sometimes I flew around with my monstie just to admire the view. Plus, the flight control was done exceptionally well, which made flying a fun experience.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2791583631
[h3]Gotta keep on exploiting them weaknesses[/h3]
MHS2 took a complete 180 from the regular MH gameplay, from the staple action-oriented to a turn-based RPG. The combat uses three attack types: power, speed, and technical where each one is weak against the type next to it. Frankly speaking, “it’s a rock, paper, and scissors” game; however, it is layered with several other elements that make each fight a unique experience. Learning each enemy behavior can be a make or break during late-game hunts. Preferably, you’d aim for a double attack, which triggers when both you and your monstie exploit the enemy's weakness, but there are fights where the enemy attacks twice or even three times on the same turn, so that’s another element to consider before choosing which move to use. What’s more, during combat, there’s a possibility to trigger a minigame that allows you to deal extra damage and fill up the kinship gauge or skill bar, which can be used to turn the tide in your favor. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2791582586
There are several issues regarding the combat system, the first one would be that the damage your character deals is extremely low, even with exploiting weakness so, you’ll need to rely on switching monsties to get that weakness damage bonus, and the other one is that there are cases where the announcement texts are scrambled, and the last one would be the bots are badly designed. Imagine cornering a boss only to have the table turned because your partner used the wrong move – yes, this happened more than once, and also yes, you don’t have control over your partner. 

[h3]Poaching is a no-go… unless you’re doing it for the sake of bonding, then it’s a-okay![/h3]
One of the main features of MHS2 is den exploration. One thing I need to point out is that the den layout consists of a random mix of several template sections unique to the specific region you’re currently in. This gives the illusion that each den differs from one another. These dens, ranging from regular to super rare ones, allow the tamer to collect a monstie egg and, if you’re lucky, several rewarding treasure chests. Keep in mind that the RNG is strong on this one, so you will need several runs before you could actually get the egg you’re looking for. These eggs have distinct patterns and colors that help the tamers differentiate which one they’re holding to.

Monsties come with several “genes” that you can unlock by leveling them, and at times, one or two random genes. Genes are essentially a skill that each monstie has. These skills can be transferred into others in order to create an abomination to your liking. How the skill system works is rather simple, the goal is to line up three of the same color or pattern, that way you’ll get an additional bonus stat on them. Furthermore, there’s a wildcard skill that allows you to pair it with any other color or pattern called rainbow gene. Ideally, it would be best to put it in the middle, that way you’d have a wider range of options of stat bonus to rake in.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2791583614
[h3]Helloooo? Is anyone there? [/h3]
MHS2 has several issues regarding the online experience; the first thing you need to know is that it is region-locked, so you would need to apply a mod in order to have a higher chance of finding anyone to play with. The second, and probably most important thing, is that online mode is pretty much deserted – ouch!, even with the mod applied, I still have a hard time finding anyone to play with. The only saving grace of the online features is that it is still doable with bots, so there’s no need to worry about having those online-related achievements locked. While the co-op quests are extremely helpful to get an early start with your monsties collection and filling up the “field guides” (built-in monster database), the PVP is not so much. The combat system works wonders during the single-player mode; however, against other players it backfired, because it boils down to a guessing game, making fights feel cheap and unrewarding since there is hardly any strategy involved.

[h2][b]Overall[/b][/h2]
Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a nice change of pace to the highly action-oriented Monster Hunter games. it really wowed me with the visual aspect and combat system. While I enjoyed the story, Capcom could’ve toned down referencing the previous game a little bit so those that didn’t play it wouldn’t be confused. Online features aside, I had a blast playing through this one! If you enjoy JRPGs, this would be a fine addition to your library. Ride on!

MH themed creature collector

full disclosure; i havent finished the game yet

obviously the star of the show are the monsters (or monsties if theyre friendly; and im going to use that term going forwards)

monsties have base stats, as well as some variance dictated when theyre born (IVs if likening to pokemon)

each monstie has a 3x3 gene grid (youll likely have to use consumables to open up the full grid), genes provide passive or active skills (unlike the original; monsties no longer have their own innate movepools; everything they can use is determined completely by genes), they also have an element (or non element) and type (or are typeless; ill get into types when talking about the combat later)... if you match 3 of either element(/non elemental) or type you receive a 'bingo' bonus that provides a damage boost to that respective element or attack type (unlike the previous game you can stack multiple of the same bingo... and unlike the previous game a non elemental bingo increase the damage of non elemental attacks rather than increasing speed)

each monstie is hatched with some base genes, theres guaranteed genes but theres also a pool of non guaranteed genes with various rarities that a specific species can hatch with (so dont go hunting kula ya kus for non elemental boost L in the first area because they cant hatch with it)

you can move a gene from one monstie to another (the donor gets eaten or runs away or goes to live on a farm... whatever you want thematically; but functionally it gets deleted) using the 'rite of channeling' (this is a feature unlocked in the second village)... if you played the original then theres two key differences; you can move gene locations (previously if a gene was top left on the donor it would only go in the top left slot of the receiver) and you can level up genes by stacking them (up to 3 times; increasing effectiveness)

you can trigger an aesthetic change by messing around with genes; you can shift a monsties element if you stack enough to overide its base stats; its colour pallette will shift to reflect the element it was shifted to... functionally however i doubt this will be worth doing, in the original it was only worth doing for non elemental monsties... but with the bingo changes (specifically non elemental bingo) its essentially gimping them for aesthetics (but the option is there if you want it i guess)

not every monster in the game is a rideable monstie, theres small monsters like velociprey that arent (because theyre smaller minions of possible monsties; ex velocidrome)... but theres also some 'big' monsters that arent possible monsties (like tetsucabra)... as far as i can tell the whole roster (sans dlc) from the first game made it across to this one, the new additions are mostly monsters that debuted in MH World; the ones that arent are either the fated 4 from generations or variations on the previous roster like bloodbath diablos or dreadqueen rathian); the total count of monsties is supposedly 81 if the monstiepedia is to be believed

Combat

so theres 4 types of attacks

speed beats power

power beats technical

technical beats speed

and then theres typeless attacks that dont interact with that system at all

this rock paper scissors forms a contentious point; and was often used to detract from the first game... which i disagreed with then because monsters (note the terminology; im not talking about monsties) had their own patterns (for example; p.rathian used to have something like 2 speed 1 power 2 speed 1 power pattern; and if you figured that out you could win 100% of head to heads)... monster hunter stories 2 has sort of dumbed that down (atleast as so far as ive gotten)... monsters have a base type (say technical), when they enrage they change their attack type (say to speed)... and rarely monsters have a third change; say inflate into a beach ball (zamtrios) or get charged with electricity where they change to the third type... its a bit simplistic

you have complete control over the protagonist; your monstie on the other hand does what it wants to do... you can wrangle them into using a learned skill on a select target but this will cost some kinship; which is an in battle resource generated through various actions (and when full can be consumed to jump on top of your monstie; which enables powerful kinship attacks); realistically if you know what you're doing then youll essentially have full control at all times though

for equipment the player character has a talisman slot (which if you're familiar with mainline monster hunter games; just provides passives), an armour slot (just one; the whole set; which provides defenses as well as more passives... in the first game if your equipment matched your monstie then you received a kinship cost reduction; i havent verified if thats still the case in this one though) and 3 weapon slots (which you can swap to at will in combat)

in monster hunter fashion; your equipment is scavenged from the corpses of your enemies (except not really because somehow you can beat a bulldrome; takes its skull... it still gets up and retreats to its den... where you can take its skull again)

each weapon is either slashing (greatsword, sword and shield), piercing (bow, gunlance) or blunt (hammer, hunting horn); some monsters/parts are weak/resistant to certain types of weapons... this only extends to riders though and each specific weapon has its own moveset meaning they play a little bit differently; for example hammer and horn are both blunt weapons but where the hammer has skills that benefit from specific ailments on the target or just deal damage; hunting horn has songs in its skills; which provide buffs, debuffs or unique effects (if you're familiar with the mainline monster hunter games the same 'this horn plays these songs' applies) (if you're familiar with the original; hunting horn had a massive rework in that you dont need to 'play' the notes by losing head to heads; you can just play the song outright for kinship cost)

you can break monster parts for big monsters; depending on the monster and the part this will have various effects; opening them up for damage, preventing them from using a move, tripping them... but sadly theres no visual indicator of this; if you break pukei pukeis tail it doesnt fall off line in the mainline games; theres no difference in the model; itll just stop it from using a specific attack

Visual

charming aesthetic, but graphically lacking, im sure it looks fine on switch but for pc the textures are a bit low quality (some in particular) and theres a very low grass LoD

Story

eh, theres some small inconsistencies across the games... also no one seems to bat an eye at the fact that 4 years before this game there was a legendary rider that saved the world from a 'blight' with a rathalos called 'ratha' (MHS1)... but also the MHS2 protags grandfather (called 'Red', which almost seems like a pokemon callout) had a rathalos ALSO called 'ratha' who become a guardian of the starting island (chronologically way before the MHS1 'ratha' but still no connection)... oh and we arent done; for some reason the razewing rathalos the protagonist hatches is also by default called 'ratha'... youd think that one of the multiple characters (including the annoying cat) that spanned both games would atleast mention this... literally no one does (atleast as far as i am in the game)... its not even a placeholder name that you can change; it has to be 'Ratha'... its weird and i cant wrap my head around it... aside from that its a meh story; its not good, its not particularily bad... but its also not why i play these games

Audio

voice acting is lacklustre at best; it also doesnt help that the english VA doesnt match mouth movements; i switched to japanese VA before eventually turning sound off altogether so i cant really comment on the score other than it wasnt gripping me

Some years ago I wanted to play a Monster Hunter game on pc so bad, but I knew that my pc was a potato and it couldn't run Monster Hunter World. So I looked for alternatives, and I found that there was a MH game adapted to Android called Monster Hunter Stories. 
At first glance the anime style it had kinda put me off, it was very different from the aesthetic of the other MH games that I knew, and it was a turn based game, very different. Nonetheless I gave it chance and it blew my mind, the game was pretty good. I had more fun with that game than I had with any other game of that same style. 
So I completed it and some time later Monster Hunter Stories 2 was announced. It greatly surprised me that the developers decided to make another game, because I knew that the first one wasn't exactly the greatest hit in terms of sales, although it had a solid fan base. Now that I had the opportunity to play this game I appreciate the developers even more, they improved upon the first game in many ways and added many quality of life features. I really hope that this game sold well enough to see a third part in the future.

A quick tip for anyone who wants to play this game: Put the voices in japanese with english subtitles. In my opinion Navirou's voice sounds way better in japanese, also Reverto's voice sounds more badass.

Btw, I noticed that the most voted reviews are the ones that complain about a bug the game had, but that bug was patched a long time ago.

This is essentially an alternative for all who are interested in the Monster Hunter franchise for its world, but might not like the combat in the main games. That’s the case for me hence I’m really glad they made this game.
First up visuals and audio are high quality as expected of the developer and franchise.
Aside from little tweaks here and there, as well as the combat system obviously, this game acts much like any other Monster Hunter game with gathering, crafting, etc. except it’s also a creature collector! From what I know it is not uncommon to run around town quite a bit in other Monster Hunter games making new stuff and optimizing your current build, which is very much the same here as well if you care about these things.
In terms of fashion, a topic I quite enjoy, it’s as great as other Monster Hunter games or in other words simply fabulous. There is a wide variety of armour, all different looking and customizable in terms of colour, you could easily put on a fashion show in the game.
The monsters too look really nice and even if they are basically just shrunken down versions of the grown monster, the freshly hatched versions are so adorable! I adore them all.
While this is technically a sequel, you don’t need to have played the first Monster Hunter Stories to follow what’s going on in this game, you’d just miss out on a few easter eggs and call-backs but nothing major. Personally I watched the first season of the anime which covers the story of the first game, so I was able to pick up on them no problem.
One gripe I do have is how grindy the game becomes if you want to actively build either many of your Monstie or even just the legendary ones you only get from special instances, which can be pretty tough in difficulty. Perhaps a difficulty slider for those would be a good idea or upping the spawn rate of super rare dens (currently they barely appear more than maybe once for every player) after finishing the story.
To sum it up this is a lovely alternative to other Monster Hunter games and as it is practically a perfect game for me personally I definitely recommend it.

[h1]Denuvo was removed.. only for Enigma DRM to be added.[/h1]
[i]This has been edited in respect to the aftershock of Enigma's introduction. Original parts of this review that are no longer 100% accurate have been stricken out.[/i]

Fun game, problematic practices.

CAPCOM has proven they have no interest in the consumer's enjoyment of their products, with the abysmal state of Wilds, and the debacle that was introducing Enigma DRM to the vast majority of their library.

On its first injection into titles like MH:Rise, RE:Revelations, and Dragon's Dogma, many users were outright locked out of being able to play due to Enigma's [i]aggressive[/i] anti-modification measures blocking out Linux and Steam Deck users, along with even cosmetic or game-fixing mods.

[strike]There are ways to get around it, including the Ol' Reliable, but this can't be overstated enough: CAPCOM's decision to add in gamebreaking DRM to more of their games, of course, is breaking the games it's added to.[/strike]

[i]Some hotfixes over the course of 2024 have "largely" fixed the drastic impact this new DRM had on the game. Steam Deck users have been reporting that they're able to access the game again - which is fantastic - and visual/save corruption fixing mods are once more able to function.[/i]

In their infinite wisdom, CAPCOM made it so that you can only play with other players in your Download Region, because everybody loves internationally-available, online compatible titles having completely arbitrary region locking.

A very popular mod fixed this anti-consumer decision that CAPCOM themselves has refused to address launch (despite a sleu of complaints from players across the globe), but since Enigma is an aggressive DRM, it outright prevents mods being added to the game, meaning you can [b]no longer play with friends who aren't in your country.[/b]

[i]This is still accurate, insofar as the original Matchmaker Region Unlocker mod on Nexus was taken down once Enigma was put into place. Removing Denuvo had actually broken its functionality, and there currently (well over a year later) is no alternative. Cross your fingers that changing Steam's download region will work for you and your friends, I guess.[/i]

[strike]This of course also means that Linux and Steam Deck users, just like with Monster Hunter: Rise, and can no longer play the game they paid for, because the anti-cheat aggression in Enigma also treats any "non-standard" or third-party parallel software the same as hacking the game files to cheat.[/strike]

I still don't recommend purchasing CAPCOM developed or published products. They don't deserve your hard-earned money when they can, with absolutely zero notice, completely block access/greatly decrease performance and usability to any game you've paid for [i]years[/i] down the line.

It ultimately doesn't matter that the product now functions (somewhat) as intended again, because the premise Enigma has set is a dangerous one to customer-product accessibility and security.

I'm not a Monster Hunter player. I have no skill in that genre, the games do not appeal to me, and I'm not good with hand-based mobility and quick time or real time events. I am, as some would say, not the main demographic for a Monster Hunter game. I do however like creature collectors. They're a bit of a guilty pleasure. 

Monster Hunter Stories - both games - are really, really good if you're anything like me. It offers all of the fun of the first game with a smaller audience, but everyone I've played with over the internet was particularly nice, even if we couldn't really talk. The game is just.. nice. You can grind at your own pace and there's postgame content. The DLCs don't really do anything other then offer you customization, so it's really just.. free to play. The controls aren't bad and there's a lot of individual customizability.

MHS2 can be played effectively as a standalone, but I'd encourage you to get the first one too (especially since it just got a remaster for Steam and a port.) If you don't, that's fine, because I didn't really think about the first one all too much either. It's just a nice little game with a lot to offer and none of the pressure that comes with the mainline games. 

If you've read this far, I hope this review offers you something of worth. If you buy the game, I hope we can meet online - I love helping people complete the postgame content :]

Everything feels satisfying. Only minor complaints I have are the damn cat and how it calls me buddy, as well as there not being a way to add ornamentation to your monsters so they can be set apart from the rank and file. That's it. Nitpicking really.

Pokemonster Hunter 2 is a surprisingly fun spin off idea that I would love to see more of in the future.

Tons of monsters to collect and gear to craft from them including some monsters I personally haven't seen before in the series. Fun ways to mix and match stats and skills on your pets and a lot of sweet cinematic attacks sometimes involving multiple characters.

The game world is cartoonish but still looks really nice. The art and audio are a huge step up from the previous game. There are a ton of other little improvements from the first one but my favorite part is that I can play on Steam!

Fun game but you can get a bug that permanently prevents your save file from being able to access multiplayer quests in any capacity, whether you want to play with another person or just do it solo.  Nobody knows what causes the bug, Capcom is unlikely to fix it.  The only solution is to start over, the earliest you can tell if the bug has affected your save file is around 5 hours into the game if you are rushing.  Not sure if your save file can just magically corrupt itself at any point, but the prospect of permanently losing out on the ability to access all multiplayer (this includes the upcoming Kulve Taroth update) because of a bug that capcom doesn't feel like addressing doesn't sound too enticing to me. [b][i]Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin[/i][/b] follows the story of you, the player, as you go through the rites of becoming a Monster Hunter on a fateful day in Mahana Village.  Of course, not everything goes to plan, as shimmering red light can be seen on the horizon.  You quickly go into the woods and after a lot of story, you are entrusted with Ratha's egg by Ena.  You go back to the village and start your adventure.  In terms of the story, it was pretty good up until the part where [spoiler]Ratha gains the ability to Fly[/spoiler], and then it's kind of just filler until the last hour or two.  The [spoiler]main villian of the game is very easy to predict who it will be[/spoiler] and the last bosses of the game aren't that difficult.  Overall, the story was pretty good, but didn't stick in my head for a while afterword.

This game is your standard Monster Hunter fare, with the exception that you are a Rider, and you form bonds with Monsties that you hatch from eggs that you gather from Monster Dens around the world.  Some are more powerful than others, and some have more useful skills than others.  There are quite a few different locales that you can visit, but you will need to backtrack once you get Monsties with certain skills so that you can go through and collect everything in the previous areas.  This part kind of aggravated me a little bit.  Monsties also come with a grid of Genes that indicate the abilities and supports that they have.  It is a 3x3 grid, and usually, there are some spots that cannot be opened, and there are some spots that you will have to unlock either through leveling or various other means.  Again, some Genes are harder to come by than others, and certain Genes can only be found on certain monsters (more on this later).  Eventually, you will learn to combine these Genes together (of the same time) of the same type to increase their power, and also be able to move Genes from one Monstie to another, sacrificing the Monstie you are moving the Gene from in the process.  There is a book of Genes that you can fill out, but you won't be able to fill it out until late into the Post-Game.  This is where my sticking point was.  I only had two or three genes left, however, the Monsties that I needed to genes from have all sorts of other genes, and ALSO only show up in Rare Monster Dens, which are quite a lot rarer than regular Monster Dens.  On top of that, they have a low chance of actually having the Genes that I was looking for.  I ended up stopping playing this game needing only 3 Genes to complete my Gene Book.

This game has you playing with yourself and an NPC, which brings into clear focus a lot of problems when it comes to the AI of your partner...they can decide to waste valuable healing items on you when you can handle the healing and other quirks like that, but they are competent enough during the main story and even the post-game that this shouldn't cause you any issues.  You get a variety of partners to choose from by the end of the game and post-game, and each of them have their own strengths and weaknesses.

This game has online missions that you can complete with other players, however, since this game came out so long ago, there is usually no one in the lobby that would be willing to help you defeat some of the hardest online missions in the game, but I was able to get by with AI partner on almost every online mission.

The main sticking point that a lot of people have is with the current DRM incorporated into the game, The Enigma Protector, which is a Russian run company.  I have spent probably 50-70 hours reading up about this DRM and the company itself, and I have seen a lot of arguments for both sides (it being malware and it not really doing much).  The main thing it does is prevent modding.  I am neutral on this point.

So, pros, neutral, cons:

Pros:

I really wish I could recommend this game, as it has a lot of great features and was pretty fun playing through. It has probably the best story of a monster hunter game (though this is a fairly low bar, as plot has never been the focus in this franchise) and a great roster of monsters, all of which you can ride and have numerous unique battle animations. However, the game has issues that are simply too substantial for me to look past, issues that primarily manifest themselves come endgame. 
MHS2 has a roster of about 140 tamable monsters, some types are naturally weaker than others, and they're all given a star rating to communicate this. However, in endgame, the content is primarily online, co-op or pvp, both of which necessitate a certain level of strength. With the end-game introduction of deviants and elder dragons, the number of endgame viable monsters is massively reduced. This highest tier of monster is substantially more powerful than those below it,  but is also small enough that crafting a balanced team only leaves you an option or two of monsters, entirely crushing team variety. Want a power-dragon monster? There is only one. Want a viable fire-type? I hope you like the Rath family, or Teostra.
With a roster of 140 monsters, the endgame consists of seeing the same ~15 over and over again. 
This is not helped by the surprisingly shallow nature of the gene system, where you can transfer moves and passive characteristics from one monster to another. The genes also have elemental types, and because of the bingo system, which rewards using the least variety in gene types, the optimal build for any given element of monster is always the same. You won't just see Teostra over and over again, you'll see the same teostra, built nearly the exact same way.
The game has such potential, but at the end when combat performance becomes a seriously important aspect, you'll discover most of the game's monsters and builds amount to shooting yourself in the foot, with only a very small collection of them being viable. If you do not like these monster's designs, if your favourite monsters lack the sufficient number of stars next to them, or if you want to give your monster genes that are not already colour-coded, your reward is being dead weight in a timed co-op challenge, or just losing pvp matches outright.

TLDR: Game plays like a Pokemon game but better.  If you wished you could play a pokemon type game with deeper mechanics, you'll enjoy this game.  At 50% discount or more, it's absolutely worth the purchase.

The base game mechanics have a few layers of rock/paper/scissors type mechanics and battles will consist of you, your monster, your AI companion and their monstie (if they have one) vs 1-4 enemies.  Each monster has their own strengths and weaknesses against other elements.  I felt like this could be largely ignored during the main story quest, but became something I had to pay attention to in post-game content.  Your hunter can use 3 different classes of weapons (2 weapon types in each class), with each monster having weaknesses and strengths against each weapon class depending on where you target them.  Each weapon type has unique mechanics and they also have element types as well.  Every monster you beat gives you access to crafting different weapons and armour from their parts.  Breaking specific monster parts will disable them or stop them from using certain moves and rewards you with more monster drops.

Most monster attacks fall into a power/speed/technical category where power beats technical, technical beats speed, and speed beats power.  This is a mechanic you have to become familiar with and has the biggest impact on how battles will play out, allowing you to hard counter most of the enemy moves, or be hard countered yourself.  You get rewarded with resources to spend on more powerful attacks, for matching up your attack type with that of your monstie or companion if it is strong against your opponent's move choice.  There are some moves that the AI can use that do not fall into a counterable category.  You also get access to these types of moves but you then can't be rewarded for successfully hard countering.  There's more nuance to this system like comboing attacks with your AI partner's monstie or letting them combo with yours.  There is an element of RNG to this because you can't control the AI companion.  Sometimes your AI partner will consistently pick the wrong moves and you can't really do much to help them other than heal them, taunt with the gun-lance, or use a trap etc.  You will have an AI companion and their monstie with you for the vast majority of the game.  Stronger/later monsters will get to attack twice/turn sometimes (mainly when enraged) and their 2nd move is usually uncounterable or random if you can because you don't know who it will target.  

Most of the "skill" in this game comes from learning the tells and patterns of enemy monsters and how to counter them.  In post-game content, this becomes imperative if you don't want to get one-shot/totally destroyed.  Some monsters are really easy to learn, having very basic patterns while some can be quite complex and sometimes have an element of RNG - IE you don't know what's coming after this move but you can guess from their tell what the move will be at that turn if you know the enemy's tells.

There is a multiplayer component to this game that you will want to engage with if you intend to PVP or do the post-game content.  This comes in the form of vs battles, co-op dens and challenges.  You can do this content with AI companions if you can't find someone to play with.  Co-op dens, you'll want to farm to get better chances at finding rare/powerful monsties and their genes(moves and passives) that you can give to monsters in your party.  The system for inheriting moves/passives is a min/maxer's dream or nightmare, rewarding you for matching moves' type and element.  There's a degree of RNG to finding these moves though, with some monsters having a higher chance of having the genes you want, but it's still just a chance.  It's possible to farm these rare things in single player only but it will literally take you ages longer, becoming borderline unfeasible .  This content is reasonably soloed with the AI and is sometimes more efficient than playing with another human because you don't need to wait for turns etc.  The post-game co-op challenges are definitely easier with another human who knows what they're doing, but it's still possible to solo this content with the AI companion, but you will be forced into specific builds/strats to consistently have success.

If you want to play co-op content with another real human player just for the sake of it, you might have better luck looking for a co-op partner in the forums instead of hoping to join a lobby or have someone join yours randomly.  There are people playing online, but it's not very many.  I'm not sure how active PVP is but I'd guess less-so than the co-op content.

I'm giving the game a thumbs down but that's more of a general view than a specific one.  For certain, specific players, Monster Hunter Stories 2: Rise will be a ton of fun.  In short, Stories 2 is a mix of Monster Hunter and Pokemon, the idea being that you can kill monsters to get parts to make weapons and armor, similar to main line Monster Hunter games, but in a much more limited fashion.  You can also make monsters retreat, then track them to their lair and steal their eggs, then go back to town and hatch them.  Each monster, or "monstie" when they're one of yours, has randomized stat bonuses and genes that grant special attacks and may provide stat bonuses.  Each monstie has up to 9 genes, and if you get 3 genes of the same type in a row, the monstie gets a stat boost, you can give genes of monsties to other monsties by sacrificing them.  This process of defeating monsters, hatching their eggs and sacrificing monsties to power up other ones is the central and most important aspect of this game, if the idea of powering up your monster buddies via collecting the best eggs with the rarest genes does not interest then, you'll probably get bored of this game eventually, as I did.

The main issue, for me, is that the combat is fairly shallow and very repetitive.  The idea behind the combat system is essentially rock-paper-scissors, each monster uses either power, speed or technical attacks, you need to select the proper attack type to counter what the monster does, which will make the monster deal less damage to you and allow you to deal more damage.  The idea is to bring in monsties with the same attack type, because when you and your monstie both attack with the same type of attack  you have a chance to do a team-up attack, which not only completely prevents the enemy from attacking but also fills your "kinship" gauge which is used to do special attacks including "ride-on" attacks in which you ride on your monstie and use their special "limit break" type of attack.  But since you only have a handful of attacks per weapon, you wind up using the same attack again and again.  Add in that the story is pretty bog-standard "friendship will fix all our problems" positive thinking story, and I just couldn't get this one to the finish line. 

For pre-teens or kids just getting into JRPGs, this is a pretty good game and if you really love to collect things and craft the best tools you can, this game is for you.  For everyone else, I might suggest looking elsewhere.

MHST2 takes the great foundation laid down by the 3DS title Monster Hunter Stories and builds upon it. The graphics have been massively updated and while the cell-shading, colorful palettes stuck around, the character, armor, and monster designs are a little less cutesy and closer to the main series in proportion, although still with significantly less detail. This is a massive boon to the game as the design work of Monster Hunter has always been one of its (or, in my opinion, *the*) best assets to bring it above the competition.
        The turn-based combat in this game uses the attack patterns in the Monster Hunter franchise as its inspiration to prevent it from becoming too predictable and dull. While the predecessor had an element of strict memorization and even randomness to spice up combat and make it challenging, this game tries to broadcast each set of moves an enemy will make clearly which looses a lot of the difficulty and can make combat a bit boring for skilled players. I don't mind this as I enjoy turn-based monster taming games primarily as a lower-effort engagement brightened by strong creature designs and longer-term goals, which MHST2 is perfect for, but if your main complaint about monster taming games is that few are as high engagement and challenging as Shin Megami Tensei you're looking in the wrong place. 
      Fans of franchises like Digimon, Pokemon, or Yokai-Watch will find that the beautiful and varied monsters and their interesting and unique animations, the wide and varied selection of armors and weaponry, and easier gameplay feeds their needs very well. In fact, if your main gripe about those games is that you can't explore the colorful and interesting worlds flying on the back of a Birdramon or leaping up cliffs on a Gogoat, this is exactly the game for that itch. Pokemon Let's Go Pikachu and Eevee took a lot of inspiration from the first game in this series to implement their own follow/ride mechanics and this still stands as the strongest representation of that.  If you love games that let you feel like you can really get attatched to your mounts or pets, this is for you.

Monster Hunter Stories was a game I had been looking forward to for a long time. As a huge fan of the main Monster Hunter games, the idea of befriending and fighting alongside the very monsters I had spent countless hours hunting was incredibly exciting. On top of that, the promise of a more cinematic and story-focused experience—something the mainline games have always been somewhat lacking in—made me go into this game with very high expectations.

Unfortunately, while the monster collecting mechanics and overall gameplay are genuinely enjoyable, I ultimately came away disappointed by the story. After roughly 50 hours, I finished the main campaign and part of the High Rank content before deciding that this was a good place to stop.

The story starts with a surprisingly serious premise and initially shows a lot of promise. However, it gradually becomes weighed down by low-quality anime-style humor, simplistic dialogue, and rather childish characters. Because of this, I don't think the narrative offers a particularly satisfying experience for teenage or adult players looking for a more mature story.

The turn-based combat is fun and well-designed, but it does have one frustrating flaw. During battles, the game doesn't display information you've already learned about monsters. Since many monsters can switch between different attack types, you're expected to memorize their patterns yourself. While this certainly rewards experience, it can also make longer fights feel more tiring than they need to be.

Another unfortunate downside is the online component. Due to the relatively small player base nowadays, online activity is practically nonexistent, which means some of the features and conveniences designed around multiplayer are no longer realistically accessible.

Despite spending most of this review criticizing the game, if you asked me whether I actually enjoyed it, my answer would still be yes. There were definitely moments that made me cringe, but overall I walked away satisfied with the experience.

My advice to anyone starting the game is simple: keep your expectations at a reasonable level and enjoy it for what it is. If you do that, I think you'll get the most out of what Monster Hunter Stories has to offer.

So quick, but important note, I played through MHS1 a year ago and loved it.  Being a big fan of MH since I was a kid, it was really great to be able to ride around and befriend monsters that I've previously fought.  Walking around the world and spotting a Zamtrios or a sleeping Pink Rathian made me go, "Oh shit it's a Pink Rathian sleeping on the path to the main town!  Isn't that a bit early?"  And then I proceeded to fight it and get my ass handed to me until I beat it.  It gave me this child-like excitement to run around and just see monsters in a different way.  Was it nostalgia?  You bet.

From what I can tell, the story is an improvement from the first game.  Still filled with cliches, sure, but it has got more charm and whimsy.  Something else I find interesting is that you don't need to play the first game to understand what's going on.  There are small, infrequent references and recurring characters, but nothing important so far.  I really liked how there's more rider-related characters.  MHS1 put a lot of emphasis on riders and yet... there barely felt like any.  Rider towns felt nearly void of human-monster interaction.  MHS2 improves on this front by adding monsters and humans all over rider towns; eating nearby food, flying around, nesting... the relationship between riders and monsters feel a lot more evident in this game.  Since I'm not a story person myself, I don't have much more to say.  It's enough, but not a reason I would play this game.

Gameplay is rad as hell.  The core of the combat is rock-paper-scissors (called head-to-heads), where one type of attack will beat the other.  If a monster has a tendency to use a speed attack, then you beat it using a technical attack.  Except that's not all!  While it's turn-based, combat relies a lot on improvisation.  A monster picks up a rock to block itself?  Swap to a blunt weapon to break it.  Are they not planning on performing a head-to-head?  Well, they're probably going to use an ability.  There's more to it, but the point is you have options to outplay the monster.  It gives the combat this feeling of active participation despite being turn-based.  Even if the monster deals more damage than you have health, you'll only be reduced to 1 if you win the head-to-head.  All these options allow you to scrape through fights you're under-leveled or under-prepared for.  It also opens the gates for interesting challenge runs.

What irritates me the most though is the AI partners you get for the story.  If I can get rid of them, please let me know.  If I want to take a fight I'm under-leveled for, the AI partner could potentially fail it for me.  Unless I'm spending resources restoring their hearts or get lucky with the monster targeting, they'll lose the head-to-head and get oneshot.  This leaves me no room for counterplay, which feels awful.  They also make the fights in the game go by faster, and funny enough, feel too strong for content you're meant to be playing.  In MHS1, you are always the only one in your adventure. Losing was your mistake.  Winning was your doing.  I lose a bit of this feeling with AI partners attached to my hip and that sours my experience.  I understand they're there for both story reasons and to introduce you to how multiplayer functions, but I wish you could turn them off as soon as you leave the first area.

And uh... Navirou returns from the first game.  While he no longer obnoxiously eats your battle screen whenever you think about doing anything, he is still a blight on this game.  An absolute rat.  He also tells you how certain monsters attack, which is a bit lame.  I'd like to learn them on my own through good ol' trial and error.  Wish I could turn Navirou off.

On the topic of things from the first game, the menu to hotswap between monsters on the overworld doesn't appear to be there anymore.  While I really only have to press two extra buttons to access the swap menu, it feels much more cumbersome.  Why remove it?

The Melynx market is a thing now.  For one, you have to upgrade stable size instead of just having an extremely large space right off the bat.  I don't really jive with this change.  The market also has crafting recipes.  In MHS1, you didn't need to collect many (if any) recipes, but in return, you can only take a set amount of items into each fight.  MHS2 reverses that, so it's... something.  Not really sure how I feel about it, but I'd imagine it's a welcome change for most people picking up the game.  You purchase this stuff with bottle caps, which can be obtained from special dungeons called "everdens" on the overworld.  Still have yet to form a solid opinion on these, but they're fun for now.

I rambled but maybe you got something out of it.

Also, Unpopular opinion but I really love Navirou. He just adds color and personality to the story. Given that at first his voice was really annoying, he easily grew on me. His character does nothing negative, and everything he does is in favor of you. He's not the type of side character whose actions are selfish and annoying.

Short version, the game is ok. It's neither terrible, nor astounding. I'd buy it on sale, but if you liked the last one, or creature collectors in general you'll probably enjoy it. 

The biggest positive for this game is, compared to the first, there have been a lot of QoL and mechanical improvements. It plays better, and the gameplay itself is honestly good. Not to complicated, but not "turn your brain off and mash 1 button". They also did a much better job at the pacing of available monsters, and the spread. In MHS1 you'd generally find a Monster and it's alternate at the same time time, generally making the original pointless to keep except for genes. They generally didn't do that this time, and they even gated certain monsters behind story progress, meaning you don't just roll into an area, farm for all the guys you want, and then barrel forward. Dens have also been improved with the split of regular Dens and Everdens, with regular Dens being massively smaller/shorter and thus much friendlier for grinding. Over all the game plays well. 

Problems develop outside of that. The narrative was...ok, nothing special, but about what you'd expect from a Monster Hunter plot. The major problem is with the tone and the characters themselves. From early on it seemed like MHS2 was going for a more serious tone than MHS1 (which I've compared to a Saturday Morning cartoon, not as a bad thing, but it gives you a clear image), however in complete contrast to this they added Navirou. I'll be frank, didn't like him in the first one, but he suited the story. Here? Completely out of place. His personality and jokes are completely at odds to everything else around him, to the extent that even the NPCs are confused. Which is supposed to be a "ha ha" funny joke, but is it a joke if no one is laughing? A problem that is also exemplified by Navirou is that the game keeps shoving characters from the previous game in, and they really don't need to be there. They basically exist to be "oh look it's that guy!" to the player, and to know Navirou. You could have replaced every single one of them with a different NPC and it would change very little. 

I am very happy to see that MHS3 seems to have wisely left Navirou and the previous narrative behind. Though I can see the makings of them repeating the trend of this game including a "sidekick of this zone". I yearn for the day they stop giving us a Rathalos named Ratha though, because by the next game there's going to be 4 of them, and it's just a bad name. I understand wanting to have a pre-set name for voice lines, but they could name it literally anything else. 

Worth buying on sale, but at least worth buying.

I am finally ready to do my review of the game after 200 hours and getting the platinum trophy, and boy is it going to be a long one. I'm going to do this review a little bit differently than the rest because of the grade I'm giving it so let's get started. This game is going to start off with the good stuff, then the annoying stuff, then PSA's for new players because there's a lot the game doesn't tell you, and then finally some notes for the next game for the developers to make the game better in my opinion (I know the next game has already had a release date, but I hope these things are in MHS3 coming out in March).

Firstly, my rating for this game is a 4.7 out of 5 and was so so close to giving this game 5* it is by far the closest game in recent memory that I was going to rate as highly. I want to give a massive shout out to the audio and visual fx team, and the animators for this game. What a gorgeous game, from the battle animations, to the howl of the wind through the caves. When I had my headphones on this game made me feel like I was in the area that I was meant to be in, and narratively, they did an incredible job with the look of the game. There are also many many improvements over the first game such as the day/night cycles having different items, there's no more delay when exiting a fight to fight the next enemy, or the egg battles. I love the buddy system, having another person in the party makes it feel like a party, and the removal of the battle pouch was pretty nice. I love that as you go further into the game the environments get smaller, if you're like me and you like to explore everything before moving on, it's nice to do it all up front and then have the environments get smaller as you go along. And finally the addition of the new monsties, making all the eggs a different monstie, the boss battles, all of it was amazing. Overall such an incredible game, and so close to getting 5* from me. 

I want to briefly discuss the reason I can't go completely 5* on this and it has the same problem as the first game which is that the story makes no sense, and being that I'm a big narrative guy, it still feels like the story has more questions than answers, why did Red come to these places? Why are we doing random fetch quests like getting a little girl's necklace to go to the next area, why is Ena even travelling with us if she's not part of the party? As cool as it is to see the people from the first game, why are they randomly showing up in these places and have no reason to be there, etc. It's just the lack of cohesive storytelling that makes me can't give this a full 5* and the other thing is that the main character doesn't speak, but the good reasons I listed above do far outshadow this small issue.

Now some PSA's for new players on things to know the game doesn't tell you. 
First, I recommend playing MHS1. The game is significantly harder than this one, but only took me half the time and taught me all about the items so I wasn't a novice when I played this game. 
Higher rarity eggs are typically better than the eggs being rainbow or shiny. 
Adding Genes to a monster should benefit the attacks that the monster has, so if it has a poison attack, find a monstie to transfer that has the right gene for the build you're trying to go for. In addition, there is a secret system called gene upgrading in the rite of channeling. If you have two identical genes on two different monsties, you can overlap the same gene on the new monstie and make it even more powerful and gain stars to make a gene even stronger, so don't release monsties until you know if there's a gene you can transfer. 
You can use the "X" key while you're in the quest log to mark the location of monsties on your map if there's a side quest you can't find the location of.
 If you deal enough damage to a monster and it starts drooping down and drooling it gets the "Tired" status. It is a good time to use a paintball because there is a higher liklihood the monster is going to retreat (If it's retreatable) .
 Riding your monstie when you're afflicted with a status effect like blastblight, poison or electrified gets rid of the status condition completely without using an item, and switching monsties in battle can make your buddy use a different attack if he's going to lose the Head to Head. Kinship skills can also break monsters out of their final attack, or even ground dive. 
You can accept a quest at the job board multiple times by clicking enter when you go to the job board if there are quest rewards that you need multiples of.
 Reverto is not a rider, he's a hunter, so he deals non-elemental (raw) damage regardless of the enemies weakness. He is by far the strongest battle buddy, and you're best off supporting yourself and letting him go crazy with damage.
Hunting Horns are extremely strong, and are going to be necessary in the late game. Find one with the skill called Evasion Riff it blocks all damage for each member of your party for one attack and they are vital for upgrading in the late game
Also upgrading your weapon actually deals more damage to parts on the monster. It makes them easier to break. Upgrading weapons in the early game has almost no effect because you're going to be switching weapons in the early game so often that it's pointless to upgrade until you beat the story. 
Finally, Keep your old weapons. In the endgame if you upgrade them enough, they turn into higher rarity weapons so don't sell them for money because they upgrade easier than buying the rare ones already.

Finally I just want to give a couple notes to the developer that would make this game 5* from me. 
Firstly, I think you should make the house customizable. Allow basic furniture, or trophy displaying from certain kills in the game, I think it would be a way to get people more involved in designing their houses and make them play the game more. 
Next, I think that you should make the game one riding action per zone. The fact that I have to put every single riding action in my party in case I go to a zone where I need to ivy climb, and jump, and rock smash, etc means I can't customize my party the way I want to, I'm confined to have to use all the riding actions if I want all the items. 
Finally, have a multi-character progression system. Basically, have things you can transfer to another character. It would increase replayability in the game and allow for things like a new game + mode, instead of just making the monsters harder, this would be sort of an ultimate challenge with a sliding difficulty. There's not really much point to me starting another character beyond the first one, and this would give me a reason to play another character. 

Thanks for listening, and it is well worth the money, buy it!
